title: Elementary changes between generating tuples over a local ring
statement: Let $R$ be a nonzero commutative unital local ring (a ring with a unique maximal ideal), with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$, let $M$ be a finitely generated $R$-module [def-weil-finitely-generated-module] (a module generated by a finite set), and let $c\geq0$. If $f=(f_1,\ldots,f_c)$ and $g=(g_1,\ldots,g_c)$ are ordered generating tuples for $M$, then one can transform $f$ into $g$ by a finite sequence of the following invertible operations: multiply one entry by a unit of $R$; interchange two entries; replace one entry $f_i$ by $f_i+a f_j$, where $a\in R$ and $i\ne j$. Equivalently there is a matrix $P\in\mathrm{GL}_c(R)$ with $g=Pf$, and $P$ can be chosen as a product of matrices of these three types. No freeness, independence, regular-sequence, principal-ideal-domain, or minimality hypothesis on the tuples is imposed. In particular this applies to an ideal generated by $c$ elements, viewed as a finite $R$-module. The empty tuple case says $M=0$ and uses no operations.

source.place: Tag 00DV, lemma-NAK; agent-formulated finite-generating-tuple consequence, combined with unit-pivot elimination for invertible matrices over a local ring. Motivating blueprint place: lem-pur-frame-independence.proof.md, local-ring reduction.

proof.text: Prove the assertion simultaneously for all finitely generated $R$-modules by induction on $c$, keeping $R$ fixed. For $c=0$, generation by the empty tuple forces $M=0$, so $f=g$ and no operation is needed. At every positive length the case $M=0$ also needs no operation, since every entry is zero. Hence suppose $c>0$, $M\ne0$, and assume the assertion for every finitely generated $R$-module with two generating tuples of length $c-1$.

proof.text: Write $\mathfrak mM$ for the submodule of finite sums of elements $ax$ with $a\in\mathfrak m$ and $x\in M$. The quotient $M/\mathfrak mM$ is nonzero: if it were zero, the zero submodule would surject onto this quotient, and [lem-weil-pbc-nakayama-local-generators], applied with $N=0$ to the finite module $M$, would give $M=0$. Since the entries of $g$ generate $M$, at least one $g_j$ has nonzero image in this quotient. Permute $g$ to a tuple $\widetilde g$ with $\widetilde g_1=g_j\notin\mathfrak mM$; record this permutation so that it can be undone at the end.

source.place: Tags 00DV (lemma-NAK, (2), (4), (8)) and 00E9 (lemma-characterize-local-ring, (1) iff (3)); agent-written induction on the length of the generating tuples

proof.text: Express $\widetilde g_1=\sum_{i=1}^c a_i f_i$ using generation by $f$. Some $a_j$ lies outside $\mathfrak m$, since otherwise this sum belongs to $\mathfrak mM$. By [lem-weil-pbc-local-ring-unit-criterion], this $a_j$ is a unit. Permute the entries of $f$, and relabel the coefficients in the same way, so that $j=1$. Multiply its first entry by $a_1$, then, successively for $i=2,\ldots,c$, add $a_i$ times entry $i$ to entry $1$. The resulting tuple $h$ has $h_1=\widetilde g_1$. Every operation is allowed and invertible: the inverse scaling uses $a_1^{-1}$, the inverse swap is the same swap, and the inverse shear subtracts $a_i$ times the unchanged entry $i$. Thus $h$ still generates $M$.

source.place: Tags 00DV (lemma-NAK, (2), (4), (8)) and 00E9 (lemma-characterize-local-ring, (1) iff (3)); agent-written induction on the length of the generating tuples

proof.text: Put $Q=M/R\widetilde g_1$, where $R\widetilde g_1=\{a\widetilde g_1:a\in R\}$. The tails $(\overline h_2,\ldots,\overline h_c)$ and $(\overline{\widetilde g}_2,\ldots,\overline{\widetilde g}_c)$ generate $Q$: reduce an expression in the full generating tuple modulo $R\widetilde g_1$ and its first term disappears. In particular $Q$ is finitely generated, directly by these $c-1$ elements [def-weil-finitely-generated-module]. It is an $R$-module over the same nonzero local ring. The induction hypothesis therefore gives a finite allowed sequence taking the first tail to the second in $Q$. For $c=1$ this is the already proved empty-tuple case in $Q=0$.

source.place: Tags 00DV (lemma-NAK, (2), (4), (8)) and 00E9 (lemma-characterize-local-ring, (1) iff (3)); agent-written induction on the length of the generating tuples

proof.text: Perform that same finite sequence on entries $2,\ldots,c$ of $h$ in $M$, using the identical scalars, units and pairs of indices, and leaving entry $1$ fixed. Writing $q:M\to Q$ for the quotient map, the lifted scaling satisfies $q(ux_i)=u q(x_i)$, a lifted swap interchanges $q(x_i)$ and $q(x_j)$, and a lifted shear satisfies $q(x_i+a x_j)=q(x_i)+a q(x_j)$. Induction on the finite list of operations therefore identifies every reduced intermediate tail with its prescribed tail in $Q$. Consequently the resulting tuple $k$ satisfies $k_1=\widetilde g_1$ and $\widetilde g_i-k_i\in R\widetilde g_1$ for $i\ge2$. Choose $b_i\in R$ with $\widetilde g_i-k_i=b_i\widetilde g_1$, and add $b_i$ times entry $1$ to entry $i$. These are shears with distinct indices and give exactly $\widetilde g$. Undo the recorded permutation of $g$ to obtain $g$. This completes the induction; all sequences concatenated here are finite.

source.place: Tags 00DV (lemma-NAK, (2), (4), (8)) and 00E9 (lemma-characterize-local-ring, (1) iff (3)); agent-written induction on the length of the generating tuples

proof.text: For completeness, each performed operation has its usual matrix on the column tuple: a diagonal matrix with one unit entry, a permutation matrix, or $I+aE_{ij}$ with $i\ne j$. Their inverses are respectively the inverse-unit diagonal matrix, the inverse permutation matrix, and $I-aE_{ij}$; for the last identity $E_{ij}^2=0$. If the successive operation matrices are $A_1,\ldots,A_s$, their action on the column tuple is $g=A_s\cdots A_1f$. Thus $P=A_s\cdots A_1$ is a product of these invertible $c\times c$ matrices with $g=Pf$, and conversely applying the factors of any such product from right to left gives the stated operations. For $c=0$ take the identity on the zero free module, the empty product. An ideal generated by $c$ elements is a finitely generated module by definition, so the ideal specialization needs no extra hypothesis.
